  `.agents/skills`), so with several adapters Belay plans one shared project
  and writes each artifact once, where the tools find it:
  - the **first adapter listed owns the one reference tree**, and every
    adapter links into it;
  - an instruction file several adapters place at one path (`AGENTS.md`) is
    **written once**, by the first of them listed;
  - OpenCode **writes no copy of a skill** Claude Code or Codex already
    writes where it discovers it, and links to theirs;
  - a command's `x-` skill that OpenCode would discover is an error
    (`cross-discovery-activation`) unless `opencode.json` hides it with a
    skill permission (`"permission": {"skill": {"x-*": "deny"}}`; the last
    matching pattern decides) or `crossDiscovery` is set;
  - a skill OpenCode finds in two directories (all three adapters enabled)
    is a `cross-target-discovery` warning, since nothing in the project can
    stop it.

  `crossDiscovery: separate` means each tool's tree is deployed apart: every
  adapter writes its own complete tree, and incompatible writes to one path
  are rejected (`output-collision`). The whole plan is still checked before
  anything is written.
- Generated links (from `@{...}` references) are relative to the file that
  contains them and must point at planned outputs (`broken-reference-link`).
  Markdown links you write in prose are text and are never checked.
- Discovery metadata and body are emitted exactly once. Frontmatter is written
  with a format-aware YAML or TOML encoder. Generated filenames and native
  metadata are checked against the target's schema, and unsupported requested
  capabilities are diagnosed before anything is written.

Adapter specifics:

- **Claude Code.** A skill's directory name is its frontmatter `name`. Claude
  Code still reads `.claude/commands/`, but Belay emits commands only as
  skills, never both for one command. Agent identity comes from the
  normalized name, never a rendered heading. `allowed-tools`/`tools` are
  never copied to another platform without a mapping.
- **Codex.** Belay never writes `AGENTS.override.md` to win precedence.
  Guidance below the directory a session starts in is not guaranteed to load.
  The byte limit checked is `instructionByteLimit` (11.1). Commands never use
  deprecated custom prompts or an invented `.codex/commands/`.
  `developer_instructions` is one valid TOML string; a generic `tools` list is
  never mapped to an invented field. Only the standalone custom-agent format is
  targeted. Codex's sandbox and approval settings govern execution and
  guidance can't override them; tool or model settings on a command are
  diagnosed. A command must produce both its files, and an agent's TOML must
  parse with `name`, `description` and `developer_instructions`.
- **OpenCode.** Don't assume Claude's nested loading or Codex's chain. Extra
  guidance files go through its explicit `instructions` configuration when a
  deployment needs them, never by loading every nested instruction globally;
  if shape scoping is required and can't be guaranteed, that is an error.
  Unrecognized frontmatter never enforces policy. `model` values are
  provider-qualified. Argument placeholders written in a command prompt are
  kept. `allowed-tools` is never an enforced command setting. Agents use
  `permission`, not the deprecated `tools`, mapped only when the meaning is
  equivalent: allow/ask/deny is not a tool list, and ambiguous conversions are
  rejected.

Other Belay diagnostics include `invalid-artifact-name`,
`missing-command-prefix`, `description-too-long`, `output-outside-project`,
`unowned-output`, `duplicated-content` and `unrepresentable-reference`.

### 11.6 Guarantees

- Identical source, configuration, directory state and toolchain produce
  identical bytes. Instructions combined into one file have a stable order.
- Frontmatter values are quoted and escaped for the target format.
- A missing reference target is reported instead of emitting a broken link.
- Unsupported metadata is reported instead of being claimed as enforced.
- Generated files are tracked in `.piton/manifest.json`, so cleanup never
  deletes files users wrote. Its `targets` records, for each target, the
  documentation date the generated files were validated against.
- Failures name the source anchor and property. Output stays inside its
  configured boundaries.

### 11.7 Open decisions

`spec/scope/belay/Decisions.pi` lists what is not decided. Tooling should say
it is unspecified rather than guess:

- Placement of instructions outside `shapeRoot`.
- The types of `tools`, `allowed-tools` and `model`, and their mapping per
  adapter.
- Naming: skill filename normalization, command name normalization before the
  `x-` prefix, acronym splitting and collision handling.
- Whether workflows stay compositions of the four constructs. Do not add a
  `workflow` keyword just because examples describe agent processes.
- How platform-specific adapter options are written.

Do not present any of these as settled. If your work depends on one, raise it
with the user.

## 12. Package management

Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
compile time.

- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
  root and dependencies.
- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
  `unknown-pin`.
- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
  to the project, and each package declares its own.
- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
  shown.
- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
  error.
- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).

The commands:

- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
  it.
- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
  imports the package.

## 13. CLI reference

Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
text and stdout carries the bare results.

| Command | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |

Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
and `namedArguments`.

## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript

`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:

- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
  whole specbase.
- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
  folding and selection ranges.
- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.

There is no signature help.

Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
after a `.` inside a string.

Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
extension:

- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
  line indented one level deeper.
- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
  level shallower.
- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
  else that is commented.

Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.

**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
   - Run `piton format --check`.
6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
   flag the gap.

## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec

Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:

- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
  `format` with no path or `-`.

- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.

Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
surprise you:

- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
  package.
- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
  the value on the anchor itself.
- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
  adapter `.pi` files.

# Planning

## How To Build

A Planning should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Planning should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A plain, quick list of the work still to do, as Linear keeps issues: stories written ahead of time, each saying how it will be sent, Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, or Freeform, gathered into the next sprint and sent to the agent in order, all at once.

## Description

Planning opens in a tab of its own in the body, "Planning", with a checklist icon, as a file opens, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) says, from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette's "Planning". It is a kanban board, filling the body beneath the tab bar, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) places it, from the tab bar down to the chat input and from the body's left edge to its right. Its sections sit side by side as columns, in the order work moves, left to right: "Backlog", "Next sprint", "Current sprint", and "Done", then "Findings", the last, as research says. Each column is headed by its name and count, with its actions, as the layout says, and holds its stories as cards, one beneath another. Every column is always there, whatever it holds; one with nothing in it shows its empty state, as the states say.

## Stories

A story is one piece of work, written as it will be sent: a title, a prompt, and how it will be sent. Each is a story card in its column, as the parts say, quiet and dense, as Linear keeps an issue, showing all a story shows: a drag grip at its top left; its title beside it, the card's one primary thing, in the body's text colour, wrapping onto a second line and cut off with an ellipsis only after that; and beneath the title, a single muted property row of small

### Items

a small mode picker, a pill reading its mode, "Code", "Chain",

"Spec", "Ask", or "Freeform", in that mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it; its step count and a small icon for anything attached, when it has them; and, once it has been sent, its status, as a task's is shown, at the row's right. Hovering a card shows a menu button at its top right. A story has no Send of its own, as the sprint says.
A column is too narrow to open a story in place, so clicking a card never expands it beneath itself or moves the cards below it: it opens the story in the side panel, docked at the board's right, as the layout places it and the parts draw a panel, headed by the story's title. The panel holds all an open story holds: its title, editable in place; its prompt, in a [GrowingTextInput](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input) with the chat input's highlighting, completions, and slicing, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) has, and its attachments beneath; its parameters, its mode, model, effort, and Slice, as the chat input shows them; its steps, with Add step, as its steps say; and its Spec citations, as the spec grounding says. Every change is saved as it is made. While its story is open, its card stays highlighted, its line in the theme's accent, so which story the panel shows is always plain. Only one story is open at a time: clicking another card opens that one in the panel instead. Escape, the panel's close button, or clicking the open story's card again closes it, and its card's highlight with it.

## Creating

Creating a story is quick, as adding a card is in Trello and adding an issue is in Linear: a story is added in the list it belongs in, right where it will sit. The Backlog and Next sprint each end with an "Add story" line at their foot, beneath their last card, or beneath their empty state when they have none. Clicking it opens a composer in its place: a blank story card, drawn as the parts draw one, whose title is a text box, focused, in the mode last picked for a story, with nothing else to fill in. Typing a title and pressing Enter adds the story to that list, where the composer was, and opens another composer beneath it, so a list can be written down without the mouse. Enter with the title empty adds nothing. Escape discards the composer, and whatever was typed in it, and the "Add story" line comes back; clicking away while its title is empty discards it too, and clicking away with a title typed adds the story, as Enter does, but opens no other composer. A story added this way is not opened in the side panel; its card is there to be clicked, as the stories say, once more than its title is

Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A plain, quick list of the work still to do, as Linear keeps issues: stories written ahead of time, each saying how it will be sent, Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, or Freeform, gathered into the next sprint and sent to the agent in order, all at once.

## Description

Planning opens in a tab of its own in the body, "Planning", with a checklist icon, as a file opens, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) says, from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette's "Planning". It is a kanban board, filling the body beneath the tab bar, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) places it, from the tab bar down to the chat input and from the body's left edge to its right. Its sections sit side by side as columns, in the order work moves, left to right: "Backlog", "Next sprint", "Current sprint", and "Done", then "Findings", the last, as research says. Each column is headed by its name and count, with its actions, as the layout says, and holds its stories as cards, one beneath another. Every column is always there, whatever it holds; one with nothing in it shows its empty state, as the states say.

A story is one piece of work, written as it will be sent: a title, a prompt, and how it will be sent. Each is a story card in its column, as the parts say, quiet and dense, as Linear keeps an issue, showing all a story shows: a drag grip at its top left; its title beside it, the card's one primary thing, in the body's text colour, wrapping onto a second line and cut off with an ellipsis only after that; and beneath the title, a single muted property row of small

### Items

a small mode picker, a pill reading its mode, "Code", "Chain",

"Spec", "Ask", or "Freeform", in that mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it; its step count and a small icon for anything attached, when it has them; and, once it has been sent, its status, as a task's is shown, at the row's right. Hovering a card shows a menu button at its top right. A story has no Send of its own, as the sprint says.
A column is too narrow to open a story in place, so clicking a card never expands it beneath itself or moves the cards below it: it opens the story in the side panel, docked at the board's right, as the layout places it and the parts draw a panel, headed by the story's title. The panel holds all an open story holds: its title, editable in place; its prompt, in a [GrowingTextInput](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input) with the chat input's highlighting, completions, and slicing, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) has, and its attachments beneath; its parameters, its mode, model, effort, and Slice, as the chat input shows them; its steps, with Add step, as its steps say; and its Spec citations, as the spec grounding says. Every change is saved as it is made. While its story is open, its card stays highlighted, its line in the theme's accent, so which story the panel shows is always plain. Only one story is open at a time: clicking another card opens that one in the panel instead. Escape, the panel's close button, or clicking the open story's card again closes it, and its card's highlight with it.

Creating a story is quick, as adding a card is in Trello and adding an issue is in Linear: a story is added in the list it belongs in, right where it will sit. The Backlog and Next sprint each end with an "Add story" line at their foot, beneath their last card, or beneath their empty state when they have none. Clicking it opens a composer in its place: a blank story card, drawn as the parts draw one, whose title is a text box, focused, in the mode last picked for a story, with nothing else to fill in. Typing a title and pressing Enter adds the story to that list, where the composer was, and opens another composer beneath it, so a list can be written down without the mouse. Enter with the title empty adds nothing. Escape discards the composer, and whatever was typed in it, and the "Add story" line comes back; clicking away while its title is empty discards it too, and clicking away with a title typed adds the story, as Enter does, but opens no other composer. A story added this way is not opened in the side panel; its card is there to be clicked, as the stories say, once more than its title is

It scrolls with the cards, after the last of them. Its composer, as creating says, is drawn where it was clicked, at the foot in the line's place, or at the top, above the first card, from "+ Add": a story card, as the parts draw one, its title a text box in the card's title text, with the focus ring around the card, and beneath it, muted, "Enter to add, Escape to cancel"; the cards below it move down to make room, and the list scrolls to keep it in view. The side panel opening or closing in the meantime, as a story opened from outside the board, changes only the board's sideways scroll, as far as the panel's opening or closing needs, as motion says, and shows it already settled when the tab is back; every column keeps its own scroll through it. The scroll is the board's own, kept only while its tab is open, and never saved with the plan, in `order.json` or anywhere else: closing Planning's tab and opening it again, or reloading the window, starts the board at its left edge and every column at its top.
88	The side panel is the one place anything opens: an open story, Draft stories, and Research, never beneath a heading or a card, and never in a popup or over the board. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the chat input, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. 89	While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.
90	
91	## Parts
92	
93	Everything in Planning is built from five parts, each always drawn the same way, in the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode:
94	- A list: one per column, as the layout places it, 320 pixels wide and as tall as the board, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base, with no border, its corners rounded 8 pixels, 8 pixels of padding; its heading row at its top, as the layout says, then its cards, or its empty state centred beneath its heading; its heading's status icon one per column, each always the same: the Backlog a dashed circle in the theme's tertiary text colour; Next sprint an empty circle in the theme's secondary text colour; Current sprint a half-filled circle in the theme's accent; Done a filled circle with a check in the theme's success colour; and Findings a magnifying glass in the theme's secondary text colour; each only repeating the column's name, never standing for it
95	- A story card: a box the full inner width of its list, on the theme's raised surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 6 pixels, 8 pixels of padding above and below and 10 at its sides, 8 pixels from the next; a top line with its drag grip, 16 pixels, in the theme's tertiary text colour, at its left, its title beside it, the card's primary text, in up to two lines, cut off with an ellipsis after the second, and its menu button at its right on hover and always while it is focused; beneath the title, 4 pixels below it, a single property row, 20 pixels tall, in small muted text, of small items 8 pixels apart: its mode pill, in its mode's colour, as the PromptModes colours it, its step count, its attachment icon, each when it has them, and its status and time, right-aligned, once it has been sent; and, in Current sprint, its steps' lines beneath, as its steps say; used for every story, in every column, muted in Done. Its states are three distinct steps, as the Theme's hierarchy orders them: hovering raises it one surface step, to the theme's hover surface; the open story keeps a 3 pixel line in the theme's accent along its left edge, as the stories say, whether or not it is hovered; a selected card, as the selection below says, takes the theme's selected surface in place of its raised one, hovered or not; and focus shows the theme's focus ring, in the accent, 2 pixels around it, over any of them, so a hover is always quieter than a selection, and a selection than focus, as the Theme orders them, and the open story's line, an edge rather than a surface, reads apart from both, a card being open, selected, and focused at once without any of the three hiding another
96	- A row: 36 pixels tall, for steps in an open story and for findings; its secondary text muted and cut off with an ellipsis, its buttons small ghost buttons with labels, shown at its right on hover and always while it is focused
97	- A panel: the side panel, docked at the board's right, full height, as the layout places it, on the theme's raised surface, its corners square, 12 pixels of padding, a heading row of 32 pixels with its name, as "Draft stories", "Research", or the story's title, and its close button, its content beneath, and its actions in a footer row, right-aligned, the primary action last; used for an open story, drafting, and research
98	- A card: a box inside a panel, on the theme's base surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 4 pixels, 12 pixels of padding, 8 pixels from the next; a label row at its top, its content, and a footer row of labelled buttons; used for proposals and for each finding's summary
99	Labels are words, never icons alone: every button reads what it does, "Accept", "Send sprint", "Start automatically", and an icon beside a label only repeats it. Each heading's count is a plain number, muted, and each status a coloured label, as the states say. The pause bar is a row across the whole board's top, above its columns, 40 pixels tall, its text and buttons on one line, the same height whatever it says.
100	Stories are selected as Linear selects issues, to be acted on together. Only a story in the Backlog or Next sprint can be selected, the two lists that take moves, as the sprint says; a card in Current sprint or Done, and a finding, never is. Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) on a card toggles it alone in or out of the selection, the rest kept; Shift+click selects the range within its column from the card last clicked or toggled there to the clicked one, inclusive, added to the selection, or the clicked card alone when nothing in that column was clicked or toggled yet; and X toggles one from the keyboard, as the keyboard says. A selection can hold stories from both lists at once. A plain click opens the story in the side panel as ever, and leaves the selection as it is. Selected cards show the theme's selected surface, as the story card above says, distinct from focus and from the open story's line. The selection is the board's own, never saved with the plan: a selected story leaves it when it is deleted or leaves the Backlog and Next sprint, as when the sprint it is in is sent.
101	While any card is selected, the bulk bar runs across the board's foot, beneath its columns, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it nor over the board: a row 40 pixels tall, on the theme's raised surface with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its top, the columns shortening to make room as it slides up in motion's quick motion, and lengthening again as it slides away once nothing is selected. At its left it names how many are selected, as "3 selected"; at its right, labelled buttons, never icons alone, in this order: "Move to next sprint", which moves the selected stories in the Backlog to the end of Next sprint; "Move to backlog", which moves those in Next sprint to the end of the Backlog; "Change mode", which opens a mode picker above it, the one a card's pill opens, setting the mode of every selected story to the one picked, their steps keeping their own; "Duplicate", which duplicates each, every copy just beneath its original, as a card's menu does; "Delete", which deletes them all after one confirmation naming how many, as "Delete 3 stories?"; and "Clear", which empties the selection. Every move keeps the stories' order, as the selection orders them, the Backlog's first, top to bottom, then Next sprint's, and animates as motion says; a move button is disabled, its tooltip saying why, while none of the selection is in the list it moves from. Moved stories stay selected, duplicates are not selected, and the originals stay so. The bar has no Send and sends nothing: a story still reaches work only through the sprint, as the sprint says.
102	Dragging a selected card by its grip carries the whole selection, in its order: the other selected cards leave their places as it lifts, their columns closing up, and the lifted copy is the grabbed card, as motion draws it, with the cards it carries stacked a few pixels behind it and their count beside its title. The gap opens as tall as the cards together, 8 pixels apart, and dropped there they settle into it in their order, all in that list, saved at once; dropped anywhere else, or cancelled with Escape, they all settle back where they were. Dragging a card that isn't selected moves it alone and leaves the selection as it is.
103	Right-clicking a card opens its menu at the pointer, the same menu its hover button opens, with the same items, acting on that card alone, in place of the browser's own; it closes as that menu does, Escape among the ways.
104	
105	## States
106	
107	Each part of Planning has the same few states, shown the same way wherever they come up, so a state is never guessed from what is missing.
108	- Empty: a single muted line, centred in the column beneath its heading, saying what is missing and what to do, as "Nothing planned. Drag stories here, or press Ctrl+N.", with no illustration
109	- Loading: a spinner and a short muted label of what is happening, as "Drafting stories…", in the place the result will appear, never a blank space
110	- Paused: a story whose task is paused shows "Paused" as its status, in the theme's warning colour, with a small pause icon, and a "Resume" button on its card, as the PromptSending says of pausing; a sprint with any story paused says so in its heading, as "1 paused", in the same colour
111	- Error: a line in the theme's error colour, saying what went wrong in plain words, with what the harness or the application reported beneath it collapsed under "Details", and a "Try again" button where trying again can help
112	A story's status on its card is the same coloured label a task has, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says, Queued, Running with its spinner and time, Done, Failed, Cancelled, Paused, or, where its task can't be found, Task missing, as the sprint says, and a story not yet sent shows nothing there, so its absence means "not sent".
113	Each part shows each state that can come up for it, worded for it:
114	- Story list: empty, "Nothing planned. Press Ctrl+N to add a story." in Next sprint, "Nothing waiting." in the Backlog, "No sprint under way. Send sprint to start one." in Current sprint, and "Nothing done yet." in Done; loading, while the plan is read on opening, a few skeleton cards in each column, never an empty column; error, when the plan can't be read or saved, saying which file and why, with "Try again"
115	- Research and its findings: loading, the live line of what it is reading with its spinner; empty, "No findings yet." in Findings; error, the run's failure with "Try again", which keeps the question in its box; a finding that ended early, as stopped, marked "Incomplete", muted, in its row
116	- Pause: the pause bar, in the theme's warning colour, as the paused section says, and the sprint's Send buttons disabled with their tooltips saying why; a sprint that can't start for a failed story says so in its heading, in the same colour
117	- Proposals: loading, the drafting line and spinner; empty, "No stories proposed." with "Draft again"; error, the run's failure with "Try again"; a proposal with no spec cited, in the warning colour with "Draft again", as the spec grounding says
118

Selecting another tab and then Planning's again shows the board scrolled sideways exactly where it was left, and every column scrolled up or down exactly where it was, at once, with nothing animating, sliding, or scrolling into view, as though the tab had never been left; nothing is scrolled to its start or to a card on the way back. The side panel opening or closing in the meantime, as a story opened from outside the board, changes only the board's sideways scroll, as far as the panel's opening or closing needs, as motion says, and shows it already settled when the tab is back; every column keeps its own scroll through it. The scroll is the board's own, kept only while its tab is open, and never saved with the plan, in `order.json` or anywhere else: closing Planning's tab and opening it again, or reloading the window, starts the board at its left edge and every column at its top.
The side panel is the one place anything opens: an open story, Draft stories, and Research, never beneath a heading or a card, and never in a popup or over the board. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the chat input, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. Only one thing is in it at a time: opening a story, drafting, or research replaces whatever it held, and closing it leaves nothing there. While it is open the board narrows to the space left of it, its columns keeping their width and scrolling sideways as ever when they no longer fit; the panel never covers the board, and the board never covers it. Closed, it takes no space and the board fills the tab again. It slides in and out at the right, as motion says.
While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.

## Parts

Everything in Planning is built from five parts, each always drawn the same way, in the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode:
- A list: one per column, as the layout places it, 320 pixels wide and as tall as the board, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base, with no border, its corners rounded 8 pixels, 8 pixels of padding; its heading row at its top, as the layout says, then its cards, or its empty state centred beneath its heading; its heading's status icon one per column, each always the same: the Backlog a dashed circle in the theme's tertiary text colour; Next sprint an empty circle in the theme's secondary text colour; Current sprint a half-filled circle in the theme's accent; Done a filled circle with a check in the theme's success colour; and Findings a magnifying glass in the theme's secondary text colour; each only repeating the column's name, never standing for it
- A story card: a box the full inner width of its list, on the theme's raised surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 6 pixels, 8 pixels of padding above and below and 10 at its sides, 8 pixels from the next; a top line with its drag grip, 16 pixels, in the theme's tertiary text colour, at its left, its title beside it, the card's primary text, in up to two lines, cut off with an ellipsis after the second, and its menu button at its right on hover and always while it is focused; beneath the title, 4 pixels below it, a single property row, 20 pixels tall, in small muted text, of small items 8 pixels apart: its mode pill, in its mode's colour, as the PromptModes colours it, its step count, its attachment icon, each when it has them, and its status and time, right-aligned, once it has been sent; and, in Current sprint, its steps' lines beneath, as its steps say; used for every story, in every column, muted in Done. Its states are three distinct steps, as the Theme's hierarchy orders them: hovering raises it one surface step, to the theme's hover surface; the open story keeps a 3 pixel line in the theme's accent along its left edge, as the stories say, whether or not it is hovered; a selected card, as the selection below says, takes the theme's selected surface in place of its raised one, hovered or not; and focus shows the theme's focus ring, in the accent, 2 pixels around it, over any of them, so a hover is always quieter than a selection, and a selection than focus, as the Theme orders them, and the open story's line, an edge rather than a surface, reads apart from both, a card being open, selected, and focused at once without any of the three hiding another
- A row: 36 pixels tall, for steps in an open story and for findings; its secondary text muted and cut off with an ellipsis, its buttons small ghost buttons with labels, shown at its right on hover and always while it is focused
- A panel: the side panel, docked at the board's right, full height, as the layout places it, on the theme's raised surface, its corners square, 12 pixels of padding, a heading row of 32 pixels with its name, as "Draft stories", "Research", or the story's title, and its close button, its content beneath, and its actions in a footer row, right-aligned, the primary action last; used for an open story, drafting, and research
- A card: a box inside a panel, on the theme's base surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 4 pixels, 12 pixels of padding, 8 pixels from the next; a label row at its top, its content, and a footer row of labelled buttons; used for proposals and for each finding's summary
Labels are words, never icons alone: every button reads what it does, "Accept", "Send sprint", "Start automatically", and an icon beside a label only repeats it. Each heading's count is a plain number, muted, and each status a coloured label, as the states say. The pause bar is a row across the whole board's top, above its columns, 40 pixels tall, its text and buttons on one line, the same height whatever it says.
Stories are selected as Linear selects issues, to be acted on together. Only a story in the Backlog or Next sprint can be selected, the two lists that take moves, as the sprint says; a card in Current sprint or Done, and a finding, never is. Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) on a card toggles it alone in or out of the selection, the rest kept; Shift+click selects the range within its column from the card last clicked or toggled there to the clicked one, inclusive, added to the selection, or the clicked card alone when nothing in that column was clicked or toggled yet; and X toggles one from the keyboard, as the keyboard says. A selection can hold stories from both lists at once. A plain click opens the story in the side panel as ever, and leaves the selection as it is. Selected cards show the theme's selected surface, as the story card above says, distinct from focus and from the open story's line. The selection is the board's own, never saved with the plan: a selected story leaves it when it is deleted or leaves the Backlog and Next sprint, as when the sprint it is in is sent.
While any card is selected, the bulk bar runs across the board's foot, beneath its columns, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it nor over the board: a row 40 pixels tall, on the theme's raised surface with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its top, the columns shortening to make room as it slides up in motion's quick motion, and lengthening again as it slides away once nothing is selected. At its left it names how many are selected, as "3 selected"; at its right, labelled buttons, never icons alone, in this order: "Move to next sprint", which moves the selected stories in the Backlog to the end of Next sprint; "Move to backlog", which moves those in Next sprint to the end of the Backlog; "Change mode", which opens a mode picker above it, the one a card's pill opens, setting the mode of every selected story to the one picked, their steps keeping their own; "Duplicate", which duplicates each, every copy just beneath its original, as a card's menu does; "Delete", which deletes them all after one confirmation naming how many, as "Delete 3 stories?"; and "Clear", which empties the selection. Every move keeps the stories' order, as the selection orders them, the Backlog's first, top to bottom, then Next sprint's, and animates as motion says; a move button is disabled, its tooltip saying why, while none of the selection is in the list it moves from. Moved stories stay selected, duplicates are not selected, and the originals stay so. The bar has no Send and sends nothing: a story still reaches work only through the sprint, as the sprint says.
Dragging a selected card by its grip carries the whole selection, in its order: the other selected cards leave their places as it lifts, their columns closing up, and the lifted copy is the grabbed card, as motion draws it, with the cards it carries stacked a few pixels behind it and their count beside its title. The gap opens as tall as the cards together, 8 pixels apart, and dropped there they settle into it in their order, all in that list, saved at once; dropped anywhere else, or cancelled with Escape, they all settle back where they were. Dragging a card that isn't selected moves it alone and leaves the selection as it is.
Right-clicking a card opens its menu at the pointer, the same menu its hover button opens, with the same items, acting on that card alone, in place of the browser's own; it closes as that menu does, Escape among the ways.

## States

Each part of Planning has the same few states, shown the same way wherever they come up, so a state is never guessed from what is missing.
- Empty: a single muted line, centred in the column beneath its heading, saying what is missing and what to do, as "Nothing planned. Drag stories here, or press Ctrl+N.", with no illustration
- Loading: a spinner and a short muted label of what is happening, as "Drafting stories…", in the place the result will appear, never a blank space
- Paused: a story whose task is paused shows "Paused" as its status, in the theme's warning colour, with a small pause icon, and a "Resume" button on its card, as the PromptSending says of pausing; a sprint with any story paused says so in its heading, as "1 paused", in the same colour
- Error: a line in the theme's error colour, saying what went wrong in plain words, with what the harness or the application reported beneath it collapsed under "Details", and a "Try again" button where trying again can help
A story's status on its card is the same coloured label a task has, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says, Queued, Running with its spinner and time, Done, Failed, Cancelled, Paused, or, where its task can't be found, Task missing, as the sprint says, and a story not yet sent shows nothing there, so its absence means "not sent".
Each part shows each state that can come up for it, worded for it:
- Story list: empty, "Nothing planned. Press Ctrl+N to add a story." in Next sprint, "Nothing waiting." in the Backlog, "No sprint under way. Send sprint to start one." in Current sprint, and "Nothing done yet." in Done; loading, while the plan is read on opening, a few skeleton cards in each column, never an empty column; error, when the plan can't be read or saved, saying which file and why, with "Try again"
- Research and its findings: loading, the live line of what it is reading with its spinner; empty, "No findings yet." in Findings; error, the run's failure with "Try again", which keeps the question in its box; a finding that ended early, as stopped, marked "Incomplete", muted, in its row
- Pause: the pause bar, in the theme's warning colour, as the paused section says, and the sprint's Send buttons disabled with their tooltips saying why; a sprint that can't start for a failed story says so in its heading, in the same colour
- Proposals: loading, the drafting line and spinner; empty, "No stories proposed." with "Draft again"; error, the run's failure with "Try again"; a proposal with no spec cited, in the warning colour with "Draft again", as the spec grounding says

8	
9	The theme is defined by its dark mode, built around a base grey of #444444. 10	
11	## Hierarchy
12	
13	How far a colour is from the base, in contrast, says how much it stands out, and that holds everywhere. The base is the quiet ground of the window. A step away is structure: panels, controls, and the lines between them. Further away is what is worked on: text, content, and the wells that hold it. Nothing structural is ever further from the base than the content it frames, and nothing decorative is ever as far as state. 14	
15	## Surfaces
16	
17	Each surface in dark mode, then light mode:
18	
19	- well, #2e2e2e, then #f5f5f5: where content is read or written, such as the editor, code blocks, and answers; the most contrast with the text it holds
20	- recessed, #383838, then #e8e8e8: text inputs, lists, and trees, a step toward the well
21	- base, #444444, then #d0d0d0: the window, its panels, and the sidebar; the ribbon has its own, as its scope says
22	- raised, #4e4e4e, then #dadada: buttons, tab bars, headers, and cards, a small step toward the viewer

26	- overlay, #4a4a4a, then #dcdcdc: floating surfaces, such as menus, popovers, tooltips, the completion menu, and inset panels
27	
28	## Light Mode
29	
30	Light mode reads the dark ladder on a light base of #d0d0d0. Wells and inputs go lighter, toward white, so they keep the most contrast with the dark text they hold, just as they are darker in dark mode for the same reason. Raised controls and floating surfaces go a smaller step lighter too, so they still come forward, and hover goes further the same way. Pressed and selected go darker, and so do lines. Text is dark on light.
31	
32	## Text
33	
34	Text in dark mode, then light mode:
35	
36	- primary, #ebebeb, then #1e1e1e: the foreground, for anything read
37	- secondary, #c4c4c4, then #454545: what the spec calls muted, such as paths, counts, and descriptions
38	- tertiary, #9c9c9c, then #636363: dimmer than muted, such as help text and placeholders
39	- disabled, #7a7a7a, then #8c8c8c: what can't be used now
40	
41	## Lines
42	
43	Lines are one pixel, and quieter than anything they separate:
44	
45	- line, #3a3a3a, then #bdbdbd: dividers between areas, table rows, and list rows
46	- edge, #2a2a2a, then #a6a6a6: the border of controls, inputs, and floating surfaces, darker than the base in both modes, what the spec calls the border colour
47	
48	A line is never doubled. Wherever two things that each have a border meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side: one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too, such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.
49	
50	## Accent
51	
52	One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection, focus, or the primary action:
53	
54	- accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
55	- accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
56	- selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text
57	
58	What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring colour, is the accent.
59	
60	## Status
61	
62	Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every surface lighter than it in light mode:
63	
64	- success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
65	- warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
66	- error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
67	- information, the accent: running, informational notes
68	
69	Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:
70	
71	- purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
72	- cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78
73	
74	Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's: blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error, purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.
75	A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the text on it below its contrast.
76	
77	## Chart Colours
78	
79	The theme has a set of chart colours, for anything that tells kinds apart in a chart, such as a task's time breakdown: nine hues, in a fixed order, blue, amber, teal, violet, rose, lime, sky, orange, and a neutral grey for "other", each readable on the theme's surfaces in both dark and light mode, set apart from one another in lightness as well as hue so they can still be told apart by someone who can't tell some hues apart, and distinct from the modes' colours and the status colours, so a chart is never read as a mode or a state. They follow the theme's brightness as its other colours do. A chart takes them in order and keeps each kind to the same colour wherever it is shown.
80	
81	## Bevel
82	
83	A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a table's header, can have the theme's bevel: a very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface, 8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and 3% in light mode, far subtler than the light and never reading as a line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border in the sense of lines never being doubled.
84	A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are barely darker and its bottom and right edges a touch lighter.
85	
86	## Elevation
87	
88	Floating surfaces sit on the overlay surface with an edge border, and are the only things with a shadow: soft, short, and black, stronger in dark mode than in light. Behind a modal surface, such as an inset panel, the window is dimmed with black, 40% in dark mode and 25% in light mode.
89	
90	## Contrast
91	
92	However the colours are used, primary and secondary text keep at least 4.5 to 1 against the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, and primary text at least 4 to 1 on controls in any state. Tertiary text, status colours, and the accent keep at least 3 to 1 on the base. Edges keep about 1.5 to 1 against the base, and lines less. Only near the middle grey, where brightness brings the base, is less kept, as brightness says.
93	
94	## Brightness
95	
96	The whole interface can be made lighter or darker, from the Brightness slider of the ribbon's Application tab, without changing how it reads. Brightness moves the mode's whole ladder of neutral greys together, by the same amount in lightness, every surface, line, and overlay with
97	
98	### It
99	
100	the ribbon's greys, the file tree's darkest surface, the wells, the
101	
102	base, raised, hover, pressed, and selected surfaces, and the scrollbar, since it is laid over them. Their order never changes: in dark mode what is lighter than what it sits on stays lighter, however bright it is made, and in light mode what is darker stays darker. A raised box never becomes darker than its ground, nor a well lighter than the base.
103	Each mode has its own brightness, 0 until set, each step moving every channel of every grey by one value, from 0 to 255, so the interface moves as finely as a colour can. At 0 the greys are exactly those given above. A mode's brightness stops at whichever step would first push a grey below black or above white, and where its base would cross to the other side of the middle grey, #777777, lightness 50 to the eye, halfway between black and white: dark mode's base stays below it, and light mode's on it or above. With these greys, dark mode runs from -17 to +50, its base from #333333 to #767676, and light mode from -89 to +10, its base from #777777 to #dadada.
104	The Brightness slider runs through both modes as one scale, dark mode's steps from its darkest to its lightest, then light mode's, so the interface goes from its darkest to its lightest with no switch between modes, and the base rises one value at every position, from #333333 through the middle grey to #dadada, with no jump where the modes meet.
105	Away from the middle grey, the steps between the greys stay the size they are at 0. Within 48 values of it, they narrow, all alike, easing in and out, to half their size with the base on the middle grey itself. Since the steps turn round between the modes, what is lighter than the base in dark mode being darker in light mode, this halves how far each surface moves where the modes meet, and every grey changes gently from one position of the slider to the next.
106	Text and colours keep exactly the values given above until the base comes near enough to cost them their contrast, and then move only as far toward white, in dark mode, or black, in light mode, as it takes to keep it: primary and secondary text 4.5 to 1 on the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, primary text 4 to 1 on controls, tertiary text, the accent, the status colours, and the other hues 3 to 1 on the base, and disabled text the contrast it has at 0; or, where a colour had less than asked at 0, what it had then. A colour that can't reach it even at white or black is white or black. So a mode made darker than 0 in dark mode, or lighter than 0 in light mode, changes no text at all, and primary text keeps 4.5 to 1 on the base all the way along. Near the middle grey no colour can keep all of that: text goes almost white just before the modes meet and almost black just after, primary and secondary text all but alike, and the hues paler on the dark side and deeper on the light. The text turns from light to dark at a single position of the slider, where the modes meet, never fading through grey.
107	The accent, the mode colours, and the status colours keep their hues; tints laid over a surface, such as a mode's, are laid over the moved surface and so move with it. The bevel's light and shade are made stronger or weaker as the base moves, so a bevelled surface lifts off its ground as much at every brightness as at 0. Everything takes the new brightness at once, while the slider is dragged, with no flicker and nothing laid out anew.
108	
109	## Chosen Colours
110	
111	Each mode's base, and the colours of Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask, can be chosen in place of the theme's own, in the theme editor of the ribbon's Application tab. Dark and light mode each keep their own, as the theme's own differ between them, and one never chosen is the theme's own.
112	A chosen base is the base at brightness 0, and may be any colour, tinted or not. Every other grey of the mode keeps the step it has from the theme's own base, in every channel, so the ladder is laid out from the chosen base, and brightness moves it from there. How far a mode's brightness can go follows its base, as brightness says, and the Brightness slider then runs through the steps it allows. Text and hues are kept readable against the moved greys as brightness says.
113	The colours of Code, Spec, and Ask take the place of the theme's red, blue, and green wherever a mode is shown, and a chosen Chain takes the place of the purple midway between Code and Spec. They are used just as they were picked, never adjusted for contrast as the theme's own hues are near the middle grey.
114	
115	## Gpui Kit
116	
117	The application's gpui-kit theme is set from these roles in both modes, so a component with gpui-kit's default styling follows the theme with nothing of its own: its background is the base, its foreground primary text, its muted foreground secondary text, its border the edge, its input and list backgrounds recessed, its popover the overlay, its primary and ring the accent, and its success, warning, and danger the status colours.
118	
119	## Modes
120	
121	Which mode shows is up to the application: see the [MainWindow](../../scope/application/MainWindow.md#main-window).
122
